titulo: Práctica de Inglés — Pruebas semestrales (12 de noviembre): Luz Sees the Light, texto del examen y How Can We Reduce Household Waste?

temas.nombre: “Luz Sees the Light” (My Book · pp. 205-234): vocabulary, comprehension and graphic novel
temas.explicacion:
Luz Sees the Light — by Claudia Dávila (My Book, pp. 205-234). It is a graphic novel.

Introducción literal del libro: “Luz (pronounced loose) and her friends enjoy listening to music and frequent trips to the mall. Then Luz’s neighborhood is dimmed by blackouts, and she realizes that she can’t do some of her favorite activities. While out on a walk with her new friend Robert, her neighbor Gord warns them that they need to prepare for more blackouts by becoming more self-sufficient. Luz thinks Gord’s ideas are a bit strange, but when the price of gas goes up, Luz’s mother points out that it affects everything from driving to the mall to the cost of groceries and even the new sneakers Luz has been saving for. Luz realizes that maybe it’s time to use less energy and be more self-sufficient.”

Vocabulary (definiciones literales del libro):
  • frequent — If something is frequent, it happens often.
  • sufficient — If something is sufficient, it is just what is needed and no more.
  • oasis — An oasis is a relaxing or peaceful spot in an area that is unpleasant in some way.
  • permission — If you get permission, someone who is in charge allows you to do what you asked to do.
  • installing — If you are installing something, you are setting it up so it is ready to use.
  • abandoned — If a place is abandoned, it is no longer cared for or used.
Vocabulary del temario cuya definición no aparece en las fotos del libro (significado general del diccionario):
  • ecology — the study of how living things relate to each other and to their environment.
  • conservation — protecting nature and natural resources and using them carefully so they are not wasted.
  • sanctuary — a safe place where people, animals or plants are protected.
  • recycle — to treat used things (paper, glass, plastic, metal) so they can be used again.
What happens in the story (ideas del libro, en orden):
  1. A power outage: no TV, no cooking, no air conditioning. Luz sees her neighbors hanging out in the yard.
  2. Luz doesn’t want the sneakers anymore and starts her “secret community project.” A speeding car almost hits her.
  3. She wants to turn an old patch of gravel and garbage into “an oasis in the city — a neighborhood food park.” She needs soil, plants, benches, a playground, posters and flyers, and permission from the city.
  4. She tells Robert: people could hang out, kids could have a playground, bands could play, and they could grow their own food so they don’t need to get it from other countries. Anika laughs: “there are supermarkets, Luz.”
  5. Neighbors say “Nope!”, “Not interested!” Luz tries to clean the lot alone with gloves and a garbage bag, sees rats (“Oh, GROSS!”) and says “I’m sorry… I tried!”
  6. Sad, she thinks: “I can’t do it by myself… The park is for everyone, not just for me!” Anika and Robert arrive: “NO, WE WANT TO HELP!!”
  7. They make posters and put them in mailboxes, on streetlamps and notice boards. The gang cleans, lays down grass, plants trees, is installing park benches, and old tires become new planter boxes. Gord’s idea (Car-Free Sundays) gets approved by the city. Mr. and Mrs. DeSouza share their plants.
  8. On Sunday there is another blackout, but the party “doesn’t need any electricity.” Luz takes her family to the old abandoned lot: now it is Friendship Park. “It was a lot of work, but everyone did a part!”
  9. Robert gives Luz shoes with her own designs, to say thanks for being his friend since he is new to the city.
Characteristics of a graphic novel (las podés ver en este cuento):
  • The story is told with pictures in panels (boxes), read in order.
  • Speech bubbles show what characters say.
  • Thought bubbles (cloud shapes) show what characters think: “I can’t do it by myself.”
  • Captions (narration boxes) tell time or place: “A FEW MINUTES LATER…”, “LATER THAT WEEK…”.
  • Sound words (onomatopoeia) in big letters: “BZZT!!”, “CHRRRK!”, “SNATCH!”.
  • The illustrations show characters’ feelings and the setting.
  • Like any story, it has characters, setting, a problem and a solution.
temas.microleccion:
Ejemplo con OTRA historieta (no es del examen): un cómic muestra a Tomás en un panel con un globo de nube que dice «Ojalá llueva». Arriba hay un recuadro: «THE NEXT DAY…». En el siguiente panel aparece «SPLASH!» en letras grandes.
Paso 1: el globo de nube → es un thought bubble (lo que Tomás piensa, no lo que dice).
Paso 2: el recuadro «THE NEXT DAY…» → es un caption (cuenta cuándo pasa).
Paso 3: «SPLASH!» → es un sound word.
Para vocabulario, el truco es el mismo: buscá la pista en la oración. «The library was the only quiet place in the noisy city» → un lugar tranquilo dentro de un lugar desagradable = la idea de oasis.

temas.nombre: Text given in the exam: comprehension questions based on a text
temas.explicacion:
Text given in the exam — En la prueba te van a dar un texto que no conocés y vas a contestar preguntas sobre él. Aquí practicás con textos cortos nuevos (no son el texto del examen).

Pasos para contestar preguntas de comprensión:
  1. Read the title and look at the pictures. What is the text about?
  2. Read the whole text once. Then read the questions.
  3. Go back to the text and find the evidence: the answer is usually in one sentence of the text.
  4. Main idea = what the whole text is mostly about. Details = small facts that support the main idea.
  5. Vocabulary in context: use the words around a new word to understand it.
  6. Inference: use clues from the text + what you know.
  7. Answer in complete sentences, with a capital letter and a period.
temas.microleccion:
Ejemplo con OTRO texto: «Ana planted a small garden on her balcony. Every morning she watered her tomatoes. After two months, she picked ten red tomatoes and shared them with her neighbors.»
Pregunta de detalle: How often did Ana water the tomatoes? → busco en el texto: «Every morning» → She watered them every morning.
Pregunta de idea principal: What is the text mostly about? → no es solo «tomatoes» ni solo «neighbors»: es Ana grows a garden and shares her tomatoes.
Inferencia: Is Ana generous? → pista: «shared them with her neighbors» → Yes, because she shares.

temas.nombre: “How Can We Reduce Household Waste?” (My Book 2 · pp. 253-268): vocabulary, comprehension, informational and argumentative texts
temas.explicacion:
How Can We Reduce Household Waste? — by Mary K. Pratt (My Book 2, pp. 253-268).

Vocabulary — definiciones literales del libro:
  • estimate — If you give an estimate, you give an amount or size that is not exact.
  • decay — When things decay, they slowly break down and rot.
Vocabulary — cómo lo explica el texto:
  • household waste — “Household waste includes all the trash created by the things we throw away.”
  • landfills — “When products are thrown away, they often end up in landfills. These are places where trash is buried in the ground.”
  • pollution — trash that harms the land, water and air: “You can help stop household waste pollution by following the three Rs.”
  • litter — “Many household items end up as litter in parks, forests, rivers, lakes, and oceans.” “…dispose of it properly so it does not become litter.”
  • fines — “The city of Seattle, Washington passed a law in 2015. It requires people to recycle food waste. The city fines people who do not follow the law.” (to fine = to make someone pay money as a punishment)
  • composting — “You can also turn food and yard waste into dirt. This process is called composting.” “Over time, these materials will naturally decay and turn into dirt.” Composting usually takes two to six months.
Ideas importantes del texto:
  • The average person in the United States throws away about 4.5 pounds (2 kilograms) of stuff every day. Only 1.5 pounds gets recycled or composted. About 164 million tons each year — “But this is only an estimate.”
  • Four basic categories of household waste: (1) paper, plastic, metal, and glass; (2) food waste and yard waste; (3) cleaning products; (4) e-waste, or electronic waste.
  • Paper makes up more than one-quarter of what Americans throw away. When paper rots or burns, it sends out greenhouse gases. Plastic takes a long time to decompose.
  • Litter puts toxic chemicals into the land, water, and air. Animals can get trapped in plastic or eat small pieces of trash because they think it is food.
  • Food: Americans waste between one-quarter and one-half of the food farmers produce. When food and yard waste ends up in landfills, it rots and creates methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Take only the food you plan to eat.
  • People can make mulch with leaves and grass clippings. It keeps the soil healthier.
  • E-waste contains a lot of lead. Less than 15 percent of e-waste is recycled. Don’t get rid of electronics that still work.
  • Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: “These Rs are listed in order of importance. That means the most important step is reduce. The less we buy, the less trash we produce.”
  • Austin, Texas wants to send nearly zero trash to landfills by 2040. Sweden sends only 1 percent of its trash to landfills. “Household waste is a major problem. But we have the power to solve it.”
Informational text vs. argumentative text:
  • Informational text: gives facts and information to explain or teach about a topic. Features: headings, photos with captions, charts and graphs, numbers and facts, words in bold with definitions.
  • Argumentative text: the author gives a claim (an opinion or position) and tries to persuade the reader to agree or take action. Features: a clear claim, reasons, evidence (facts and examples) that support the reasons, and a conclusion that repeats the claim or asks the reader to act.
temas.microleccion:
Ejemplo con OTRO tema (no es del examen): «Water is precious. Every person should turn off the tap while brushing their teeth. A running tap wastes about 6 liters per minute.»
Paso 1: ¿Hay una opinión que el autor quiere que aceptemos? Sí: «Every person should turn off the tap» → es un claim (argumentativo).
Paso 2: ¿Hay evidencia? «6 liters per minute» → es un fact que apoya el claim.
Paso 3: Si el texto solo dijera «A running tap uses about 6 liters per minute» con un gráfico, sin pedirnos nada, sería informativo.
Vocabulario con otra oración: «The old banana turned brown and soft» → se está pudriendo lentamente = la idea de decay.

variantes.pregunta: ¿Es una característica de un texto informativo o de un texto argumentativo?

elementos.texto: Gives facts to explain or teach about a topic
Uses headings, charts and photos with captions
The author states a claim (an opinion)
Gives reasons and evidence to persuade the reader
Asks the reader to agree or to take action

variantes.pista: Informativo = explicar. Argumentativo = convencer.

variantes.pregunta: Which feature of “How Can We Reduce Household Waste?” is a typical feature of an informational text?
opciones: The bar graph “American Recycling Rates From 1960 to 2010”
variantes.respuesta: The bar graph “American Recycling Rates From 1960 to 2010”
variantes.pista: Los textos informativos usan gráficos con datos y números.

variantes.pregunta: Which sentence from the text sounds most like an argument (a claim the author wants us to believe)?
opciones: “Household waste is a major problem. But we have the power to solve it.”
“Composting usually takes two to six months.”
“Soda cans are usually made of a metal called aluminum.”
“Sweden sends only 1 percent of its trash to landfills.”
variantes.respuesta: “Household waste is a major problem. But we have the power to solve it.”
variantes.pista: Los otros son datos que se pueden comprobar; un claim es una opinión del autor.

variantes.pregunta: ¿Es cierto que en un texto argumentativo el autor da razones y evidencia para convencer al lector?
variantes.pista: Argumentar = convencer con razones.
